title: A WeChat-delivered Information–Motivation–Behavioral skills intervention to improve HPV vaccine acceptability among Chinese gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men

paragraphs.en: Human papillomavirus (HPV) is the most common sexually transmitted infection and a leading cause of anal, penile, and oropharyngeal cancers, particularly among gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (MSM).1,2 In China, sexual minority men bear a disproportionate burden, with anal HPV prevalence ranging from 53.6% among HIV-negative individuals to 85.1% among those living with HIV.3,4 Regional studies from Urumqi and Shenzhen report anal HPV prevalence exceeding 51.8% among HIV-negative MSM and 70.0% among HIV-positive MSM.5,6 Moreover, HIV co-infection is associated with an increased risk of high-risk HPV infection and subsequent HPV-related cancers.4,6

HPV vaccination is the most effective strategy for preventing HPV-related diseases.7,8 Clinical trials have demonstrated up to 77.5% efficacy in preventing high-grade anal intraepithelial neoplasia in men,9 and international guidelines recommend routine vaccination prior to sexual debut.10 Countries such as Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States have implemented targeted HPV vaccination programs for MSM.11 However, global uptake remains suboptimal. Among Chinese gay men, bisexual men, and other MSM, willingness to vaccinate ranges from 18% to 83%,12,13 yet hesitancy persists. This hesitancy is shaped by limited knowledge, low perceived susceptibility, mistrust in vaccine efficacy, anticipated regret, stigma, lack of healthcare provider recommendations, low self-efficacy in navigating healthcare access, and cost barriers.13–15

Behavioral interventions have shown promise in addressing these challenges. In Hong Kong, a randomized controlled trial combining a Health Belief Model – based online program with motivational interviewing increased vaccine completion to 17.3%, compared with 7.2% in the control group.16 Similarly, the Outsmart HPV program in the United States increased vaccination initiation to 45%, versus 26% in the control group.17 However, culturally tailored strategies remain scarce in mainland China.

Given the limited availability of culturally tailored HPV vaccination strategies for gay men, bisexual men, and other MSM in mainland China, as well as the need for scalable, theory-driven mHealth approaches, the Information – Motivation – Behavioral Skills (IMB) model was identified as a suitable foundation. The IMB model specifies modifiable determinants that can be directly translated into intervention content and mechanisms.18,19 By contrast, prior MSM-focused interventions grounded in models such as the Health Belief Model and Protection Motivation Theory primarily emphasize cognitive appraisals and intentions,16,20 which may be less explicit in addressing the practical skills and self-efficacy required to translate intention into initiation and completion of a multi-dose vaccination series in stigmatized, digitally mediated settings.16,18 Evidence from IMB-informed HPV vaccination studies further supports its relevance for improving acceptability, intention, and related outcomes, including in mainland China,19,21 while also allowing incorporation of affective determinants such as anticipated regret.21 We therefore adopted the IMB model to guide intervention development, as it offers a parsimonious, intervention-ready framework that can be readily translated into concrete, measurable components and operationalized within social media – based mHealth programs. WeChat, China’s most widely used social media platform, has demonstrated effectiveness in HIV prevention among MSM, as shown in the WeTest randomized controlled trial, which significantly increased HIV testing uptake.22 Despite its potential, WeChat has not yet been leveraged for HPV vaccination promotion in this population.

China has recently expanded access to HPV vaccines. Cervarix® (bivalent) was introduced in 2016, Gardasil® (quadrivalent) in 2017, and Gardasil®9 in 2018, initially for females.23 In January 2025, the National Medical Products Administration approved the quadrivalent HPV vaccine for males aged 9–26 y and the nine-valent HPV vaccine for males aged 16–26 y, with market availability beginning in April 2025.24 These milestones mark a shift toward gender-neutral vaccination and extend protection to high-risk groups. Nonetheless, a critical gap remains: no culturally tailored, theory-driven interventions have been developed to promote HPV vaccination among Chinese men, even as this population increasingly relies on social media for health information.

The present study addressed this gap by conducting a randomized controlled trial to test a culturally adapted intervention grounded in the IMB model and delivered via WeChat. We evaluated whether this approach could enhance HPV vaccine acceptability among Chinese MSM, providing timely insights in the context of China’s evolving HPV vaccination policy.

The study employed a parallel-group randomized controlled trial. Eligible participants were males aged 18–45 y who self-identified as gay or bisexual, or who reported having sex with men; were residents of China; had not received any HPV vaccination; and were active WeChat users. The exclusion criteria were unwillingness to provide follow-up information, prior participation in pilot HPV vaccination studies, and inability to read or access WeChat-delivered content. The full CONSORT 2025 checklist is provided in Table S4.

A total of 684 participants provided informed consent and completed the baseline questionnaire. Participants were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to either the intervention group (n = 351) or the control group (n = 333). The intervention group received a 5-d HPV Vaccine Promotion Program (HPVVP), which delivered 12 multimedia messages focused on HPV and HPV vaccination among MSM. Content included short videos, infographics, and concise text summaries, with one to three messages delivered daily. Minimal reference was made to HIV. Participants could also submit HPV-related questions through the HPVVP consultation page. The control group received time-matched HIV-related multimedia health messages developed by the Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Outcomes were assessed at three time points: baseline (T0), immediately post-intervention (T1), and 1 month post-intervention (T2).

In January 2025, China’s regulatory authority approved quadrivalent HPV vaccination for males aged 9–26 y.24 Although current approvals focus on younger male age groups, adults older than 26 y remain a key population for demand generation and policy planning. Accordingly, an 18- to 45-y eligibility window was adopted to capture unvaccinated adult WeChat users and to generate evidence relevant to potential future catch-up vaccination expansion.

The sample size for the two-arm randomized controlled trial was calculated using a standard formula appropriate for repeated-measures comparisons between intervention and control groups.25 The expected effect size was informed by prior web-based interventions that assessed changes in HPV vaccination acceptability, attitudes, and related cognitive outcomes among sexual minority men.17,26 Assuming a two-sided alpha of 0.05 and 80% power, the calculation indicated that 57 participants per group were required for two assessment points (T0, T1), or 30 participants per group for three assessment points (T0, T1, T2).26 To account for potential attrition, a 30% dropout rate was anticipated based on attrition patterns commonly reported in mHealth interventions targeting gay, bisexual, and other MSM populations.27 To ensure adequate statistical power, a total sample of 684 gay men, bisexual men, and other MSM was recruited, with 351 participants randomized to the intervention group and 333 to the control group. No interim analyses were planned or conducted, and no stopping guidelines were specified.

Recruitment was conducted through online purposive sampling via WeChat. Advertisements disseminated by local CDC offices and MSM-focused nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) in Jiangsu Province were shared through Moments and group chats and linked to the HPVVP official account via QR code. Participants registered by clicking the “Agree” button in the system. Participation was anonymous, with WeChat IDs and the last four digits of phone numbers collected solely for allocation and deduplication purposes. Participants were informed that they could withdraw at any time. Compensation ranged from ¥20 to ¥40 (US$2.80–5.50) per completed survey. Although recruitment activities were coordinated in Jiangsu Province, WeChat’s nationwide reach enabled participation from across China.

Participants were randomized after completion of baseline assessment and eligibility screening using a computer-generated sequence produced by an independent technology supplier. Allocation concealment was ensured because group assignment was managed externally and embedded within the program backend, and recruiters had no access to the randomization sequence. Participants were not explicitly informed of their group allocation at enrollment. Implementer blinding was not feasible because of the nature of intervention delivery and backend data export requirements; however, statistical analyses were conducted with analysts blinded to group allocation.

The HPVVP intervention was delivered through a dedicated WeChat official account supported by an external IT provider. Following completion of the baseline assessment, participants subscribed to the account and received multimedia messages daily for 5 consecutive days, with daily reminders to encourage engagement. All content could be revisited during the intervention period. Participants were also able to consult a study physician privately via one-on-one chat, with responses provided within 48 hours.

Development of the HPVVP intervention followed an iterative process guided by an expert panel comprising three epidemiologists from the Jiangsu CDC, one physician specializing in MSM health education, three NGO representatives with experience in HIV service delivery, and one academic expert in social media – based interventions. Weekly meetings were held to ensure content accuracy, user engagement, cultural appropriateness, and usability. Intervention modules were refined through repeated review and testing, drawing on World Health Organization recommendations, published literature, Chinese CDC guidelines, and United Kingdom National Health Service standards. Figure 1 and Table 1 summarize the intervention flow, content, alignment with the IMB model, and delivery schedule. The names of panel members are listed in Table S5; for privacy protection, pseudonyms were used for some experts.

Baseline characteristics included sociodemographic variables: age group (18–24, 25–30, 31–40, 41–45 y), ethnicity (Han vs. other), household registration (urban vs. rural), highest education level (junior high or below, high/secondary school, junior college/technical secondary school, college or above), employment status (employed, student, unemployed), marital status (married, unmarried, divorced), and monthly disposable income (≤3,000, 3001–5000, ≥5,000 RMB). Sexual health – related variables included sexual orientation (gay, bisexual, prefer not to say), relationship status (in a relationship vs. single), disclosure of sexual orientation (yes/no), age at first same-sex intercourse (≤17, >17, never), number of sexual partners (0, 1–5, 6–10, ≥10), frequency of anal intercourse in the past 12 months (0, 1–2, 3–10, ≥11), participation in gay venues (weekly, monthly, twice a year, once a year, less often than once a year, never), dating app use (never, at least monthly, several times a year, once a year or less), age at first sexually transmitted infection screening (≤19, >19, never), history of sexually transmitted infection diagnosis (yes/no/prefer not to say), timing of last clinic-based HIV test (within 6 months vs. >6 months), self-reported HIV status (definitely negative, probably negative/probably positive, definitely positive, don’t know/prefer not to say), and perceived awareness of HPV (never heard of it, very little, some, a lot).

Psychosocial constructs and HPV vaccine acceptability were assessed using multi-item 5-point Likert scales (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree). Item responses were averaged within each scale or subscale, with higher scores indicating stronger endorsement of the construct. Internal consistency reliability was evaluated using Cronbach’s α, which reflects inter-item correlation and supports the use of composite scores in subsequent analyses. HPV and HPV vaccine knowledge was assessed using items with “Yes,” “No,” and “I don’t know” response options, scored as correct (1) versus incorrect or unknown (0), and summed to generate a total knowledge score (range: 0–13). This objective scoring was reported separately from Likert-scale reliability statistics.

The primary outcome was HPV vaccine acceptability. This was defined as willingness to receive the HPV vaccine and was measured using a six-item scale adapted from Nadarzynski et al.29 (5-point Likert scale; Cronbach’s α = 0.929).

The secondary outcomes were the following IMB constructs: Information: A 13-item knowledge scale assessing HPV and HPV vaccines, with response options “True,” “False,” or “I dont know.”16,20 Motivation: Six subscales assessed perceived severity (5 items, α = 0.936), perceived susceptibility (4 items, α = 0.949), perceived effectiveness (6 items, α = 0.860), perceived barriers (3 items, α = 0.805), anticipated regret (2 items, α = 0.829), and subjective norms (3 items, α = 0.888).21,26,29,30 Behavioral skills: A four-item self-efficacy subscale assessed confidence in obtaining the HPV vaccine (α = 0.868).16
Information: A 13-item knowledge scale assessing HPV and HPV vaccines, with response options “True,” “False,” or “I dont know.”16,20

Motivation: Six subscales assessed perceived severity (5 items, α = 0.936), perceived susceptibility (4 items, α = 0.949), perceived effectiveness (6 items, α = 0.860), perceived barriers (3 items, α = 0.805), anticipated regret (2 items, α = 0.829), and subjective norms (3 items, α = 0.888).21,26,29,30
Behavioral skills: A four-item self-efficacy subscale assessed confidence in obtaining the HPV vaccine (α = 0.868).16

Questionnaire items were adapted from previously validated measures of HPV vaccine acceptability and IMB constructs developed for gay men, bisexual men, and other MSM populations.16,17,21,26,29,30 Content validity was established through expert panel review involving epidemiology, clinical, behavioral science, and sexual minority community specialists, along with cognitive review conducted with sexual minority men volunteers to ensure clarity and cultural acceptability. The instrument was pilot-tested in November 2024 in Jiangsu, China (n = 25) to assess internal consistency reliability using Cronbach’s α, interpreted according to standard thresholds in behavioral research (≈0.70 acceptable, ≥0.80 good, ≥0.90 excellent). In the present study, reliability coefficients ranged from good to excellent (α = 0.73–0.93), with detailed estimates reported in Supplementary Table S1.

Potential confounders were prespecified as baseline characteristics collected at enrollment. Baseline covariates showing imbalances between groups were included as covariates in all longitudinal models to minimize potential bias arising from these differences. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize baseline characteristics, and between-group differences were assessed using independent t tests or chi-square tests. Relationship status and perceived awareness of HPV showed baseline imbalances and were therefore included as covariates in all models.

Generalized estimating equations (GEEs) were used to model intervention effects over time, including terms for group, time, and the group × time interaction, with robust standard errors under an intention-to-treat framework (α = 0.05; 95% confidence intervals [CIs]). As a sensitivity analysis, all GEE models were repeated using the observed (non-imputed) dataset, and the resulting estimates were compared with those from the primary analyses based on multiple imputation and pooled using Rubin’s rules.

Mediation analyses were conducted using Hayes’ PROCESS macro (version 4, Model 4; 2022).31 Randomization status (intervention = 1, control = 0) served as the independent variable (X), change in HPV vaccine acceptability from baseline to immediate post-intervention (T1 − T0) as the dependent variable (Y), and changes in IMB constructs over the same period (T1 − T0) as mediators (M). Each IMB construct was examined in a separate model. Missing data were addressed using multiple imputation, with pooled estimates reported according to Rubin’s rules. All analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics version 27.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY).

The participant recruitment flowchart is shown in Figure 2. Between November 2024 and January 2025, 1045 individuals completed the baseline questionnaire, of whom 684 gay men, bisexual men, and other MSM were randomized to the intervention (n = 351) or control (n = 333) group.

Among the 1045 participants who completed the baseline survey (T0), 310 did not proceed to randomization because they did not subscribe to the study WeChat official account (or unsubscribed shortly thereafter) or declined further participation in follow-up assessments. An additional 51 participants reported prior HPV vaccination at baseline and were excluded. As a result, 684 eligible, unvaccinated men were randomized to the intervention or control group.

At the time of study planning, HPV vaccines were assumed to be unavailable to men in mainland China; therefore, male vaccination was expected to be rare and vaccination status was not used as an initial screening criterion. The baseline survey was administered broadly to recruit a diverse sample of sexual minority men while capturing vaccination history. After vaccinated individuals were identified, they were excluded to ensure analyses were restricted to unvaccinated participants. No privacy breaches, psychological adverse events, or other unintended events were reported in either study group, and no withdrawals were attributed to harms.

The mean age of the participants was 30.4 y, with no significant difference between groups (p = .827). Most participants identified as gay (75%) and were employed (79%). Approximately 42% had attained a college degree or higher, and nearly half (50%) had urban household registration. Over 62% reported being in a romantic relationship, with a higher proportion in the intervention group (p = .013). Monthly disposable income was moderate, with 44% reporting earnings greater than 5000 RMB. More than half of participants used dating apps at least monthly, and approximately 70% reported attending gay venues, typically once a month or less. Nearly half reported no history of same-sex intercourse, while 40% reported having had one to five sexual partners. About 32% reported engaging in anal intercourse more than 10 times in the past year. Most participants (63%) had undergone HIV testing within the past 6 months, and 15% self-identified as HIV-positive. Perceived awareness of HPV differed between groups (p = .021), with a higher proportion of participants in the control group reporting “very little” awareness (41.1%) compared with the intervention group (31.7%). The groups were otherwise comparable. Relationship status and perceived HPV awareness were adjusted for in subsequent analyses (Table 2).

Overall, 69.7% (477/684) of participants had incomplete longitudinal data, contributing data at only one or two time points, while 30.1% (206/684) completed all three assessments (T0, T1, and T2). At T2, attrition rates were 65.0% (228/351) in the intervention group and 74.8% (249/333) in the control group. Attrition analyses compared completers (n = 206) and dropouts (n = 477). No significant differences were observed in demographic characteristics, baseline HPV vaccine acceptability, or IMB-related constructs (all p > .05) (Table S2), suggesting that attrition was not systematically related to key outcomes.

The GEE model showed a significant group × time interaction effect on HPV vaccine acceptability (Wald χ2 = 16.44, p < .0001) (Table 3). At T1, the intervention group reported higher acceptability (mean ± standard deviation: 3.86 ± 0.87) than the control group (3.63 ± 0.96; β = 0.42, 95% CI [0.17, 0.68], p < .001; d = 0.25). At T2, the between-group difference was smaller and marginally significant (β = 0.28, 95% CI [0.00, 0.56], p = .05; d = 0.06). As illustrated in Figure 3, participants in the intervention group showed a marked increase in vaccine acceptability at T1, followed by a partial decline at T2, whereas the control group demonstrated a modest but steady increase over time.

The intervention significantly improved HPV-related knowledge (Wald χ2 = 29.32, p < .001). At T1, the intervention group scored higher (8.43 ± 2.68) than the control group (6.87 ± 2.52; β = 1.43, 95% CI [0.70, 2.15], p < .001; d = 0.60). Knowledge gains were largely maintained at T2, while the control group exhibited only modest increases (Figure 4).

Significant group × time interaction effects were observed for perceived severity (Wald χ2 = 6.80, p = .033), perceived effectiveness (Wald χ2 = 6.99, p = .030), anticipated regret (Wald χ2 = 8.59, p = .014), and subjective norms (Wald χ2 = 12.14, p < .001) (Table 4). At T1, the intervention group reported stronger anticipated regret (β = 0.24, 95% CI [0.05, 0.44], p = .02; d = 0.12) and stronger subjective norms (β = 0.49, 95% CI [0.29, 0.69], p < .001; d = 0.68). No significant between-group differences were observed for perceived susceptibility or perceived barriers. Overall, motivational gains were most pronounced for perceived effectiveness, social influence, and anticipated regret (Figure 5).

Self-efficacy demonstrated a significant group × time interaction effect (Wald χ2 = 13.21, p = .001). At T1, the intervention group showed greater gains in self-efficacy compared with the control group (β = 0.31, 95% CI [0.12, 0.50], p < .001; d = 0.25). By T2, this difference had diminished and was no longer statistically significant (β = 0.18, 95% CI [−0.05, 0.41], p = .13; d = 0.11) (Figure 6).

For the primary outcome, the intervention was associated with higher HPV vaccine acceptability at T1 in both analytic approaches (imputed data: β = 0.42, 95% CI [0.17, 0.68]; observed data: β = 0.33, 95% CI [0.16, 0.50]), with attenuation of effects at T2 (imputed data: β = 0.28, 95% CI [0.00, 0.56]; observed data: β = 0.01, 95% CI [−0.14, 0.34]). For IMB-related mechanisms, both approaches showed significant improvements at T1 in information (imputed: β = 1.43, 95% CI [0.70, 2.15]; observed: β = 2.49, 95% CI [2.06, 2.92]), subjective norms (imputed: β = 0.49, 95% CI [0.29, 0.69]; observed: β = 0.59, 95% CI [0.45, 0.72]), and self-efficacy (imputed: β = 0.31, 95% CI [0.12, 0.50]; observed: β = 0.37, 95% CI [0.20, 0.55]). Corresponding contrasts at T2 were generally non-significant. Detailed GEE results based on observed data are presented in Supplementary Table S3.

Mediation analyses (Table 4) confirmed that the intervention significantly improved HPV vaccine acceptability (total effect: β = 0.384, p < .001). Key mediators included knowledge (β = 0.357, 95% CI [0.228, 0.487]), subjective norms (β = 0.356, 95% CI [0.288, 0.425]), self-efficacy (β = 0.324, 95% CI [0.244, 0.405]), and perceived barriers (β = 0.149, 95% CI [0.108, 0.191]). Complementary mediation effects were observed for perceived effectiveness (β = 0.157, 95% CI [0.091, 0.225]) and perceived severity (β = 0.040, 95% CI [0.019, 0.062]). No significant mediation effects were detected for anticipated regret or perceived susceptibility.

This randomized controlled trial demonstrates that a brief, IMB-guided intervention delivered via a WeChat official account increased HPV vaccine acceptability among sexual minority men in mainland China compared with an attention-matched control, with the clearest between-group differences observed immediately post-intervention. Although the observed effects were modest at the individual level, they may be practically meaningful when delivered at scale through near-universal platforms such as WeChat, particularly for preventive behaviors where population-level impact depends on reach, frequency, and low marginal delivery costs.

These findings are notable for three reasons. First, they coincide with China’s 2025 approval of HPV vaccines for males, creating immediate opportunities for public health action. Second, WeChat – used by more than one billion people in China – offers a scalable platform for precision public health interventions, with effectiveness comparable to SMS-based programs such as txt2protect.21 Third, this study demonstrates the cross-cultural relevance of the IMB model in a high-stigma context, extending prior evidence and addressing health equity gaps among gay men, bisexual men, and other MSM.19

The pattern of change across IMB-related determinants helps clarify why the intervention improved vaccine acceptability and where its practical leverage may lie. The intervention produced more pronounced improvements in theory-proximal constructs – particularly HPV and HPV vaccine knowledge, perceived supportive norms, and self-efficacy – than in acceptability alone. This pattern aligns with the IMB model’s proposition that information, motivation, and behavioral skills function as proximal drivers of prevention-related outcomes.18 Prior studies among gay men, bisexual men, and other MSM have consistently identified low HPV-related knowledge and misinformation as major barriers to vaccination and have linked perceived social approval from peers and healthcare providers to greater willingness to vaccinate, including in Chinese settings.12–16,32 Taken together, these findings suggest that mobile interventions may exert their most immediate and actionable influence by improving what people know, how socially supported they feel, and how capable they feel of navigating vaccination processes.

Mechanism-focused findings further underscore the practical significance of the intervention. Mediation analyses indicated that improvements in HPV vaccine acceptability were driven primarily by gains in knowledge, subjective norms, and self-efficacy. Knowledge emerged as the strongest mediator, highlighting the continued importance of correcting misinformation and addressing informational gaps, even among populations with elevated risk profiles, as observed in studies of MSM in Malaysia.32 Subjective norms were strongly influenced by peer testimonials and provider recommendations, consistent with the collectivist social dynamics characteristic of Chinese cultural contexts.14,19 Strengthening peer networks and community-based reinforcement may further amplify these effects. Self-efficacy also played a critical role: content addressing clinical navigation appeared to empower participants to act, although additional supports – such as financial subsidies, stigma reduction, and improved access to affirming services – are likely necessary to ensure that intention translates into action.

Interestingly, perceived barriers functioned as a paradoxical mediator. Increased awareness of barriers, particularly financial barriers, may have heightened participants’ recognition of obstacles without simultaneously offering solutions, consistent with the “cue to action” paradox described in the Health Belief Model.14 Addressing this dynamic likely requires integrating cognitive and structural strategies. Potential approaches include periodic WeChat reminders reinforcing information about vaccine access, NGO-partnered voucher programs for low-income MSM,28 and telehealth consultations with LGBTQ-affirming clinicians to reduce stigma-related avoidance of care.27 Together, these strategies could strengthen both cognitive and structural pathways to HPV vaccine uptake.

Despite these benefits, intervention effects attenuated by 1 month, which may be explained by three complementary mechanisms. First, the 5-d program may have been too brief to consolidate behavior change; IMB theory emphasizes the importance of sustained reinforcement.18 Second, structural barriers – particularly cost – likely continued to undermine psychosocial gains, especially among lower-income participants. Third, emotional constructs such as anticipated regret appeared to diminish more rapidly than cognitive gains, reflecting the relative fragility of affective motivation in digital health interventions.16,21 This pattern highlights an inherent limitation of short-duration digital health programs: brief, time-limited exposure may be sufficient to produce immediate improvements in attitudes and motivation, but reinforcement is often required to sustain these gains over time.19 In other words, initial changes may dissipate once the intervention ends, suggesting that maintenance strategies are needed to preserve motivation and prevent post-intervention decline. Policymakers and practitioners should therefore consider incorporating booster sessions, periodic reminders, or longer-duration digital campaigns.

Sensitivity analyses indicated that the primary conclusions are generally robust: short-term intervention effects were most consistently observed for vaccine acceptability and proximal IMB mechanisms, whereas longer-term effects appeared weaker. Differences between imputed and observed-data estimates for several secondary outcomes suggest that these constructs may be more susceptible to attrition patterns and to the assumptions underlying multiple imputation, particularly if missingness is related to unmeasured psychosocial characteristics or differential engagement with follow-up assessments.

A substantial proportion of participants were older than the male age bands currently approved for HPV vaccination in mainland China. This does not negate the relevance of the findings because the study focused on vaccine acceptability – an upstream determinant of uptake – during a period of rapid policy transition. Acceptability data among adult sexual minority men can inform communication strategies, identify modifiable pathways, and support planning for potential catch-up expansion or targeted delivery strategies as access continues to evolve.

These findings also help explain why short-term statistical improvements may not automatically translate into sustained or larger downstream impact in the absence of complementary structural supports. Although perceived barriers did not differ significantly between groups over time, mediation results suggested that barrier-related changes nonetheless contributed to acceptability, implying that intervention exposure may have heightened awareness of real-world constraints. Prior research among gay men, bisexual men, and other MSM in Chinese contexts similarly identifies financial burden, stigma, and limited provider recommendation as persistent obstacles, even among individuals who hold favorable attitudes toward HPV vaccination.13–16 Accordingly, the practical value of a scalable WeChat-based intervention is likely maximized when paired with implementation-oriented components that reduce friction at the point of action, such as repeated access cues, navigation to LGBTQ±affirming services, and partnerships that lower out-of-pocket costs or improve convenience.21,27,28 In this way, modest short-term improvements in acceptability can function as a meaningful first step within a broader pathway toward vaccine initiation and completion.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, recruitment via WeChat may underrepresent individuals who are less connected to online networks (e.g., some rural residents or users with limited digital access), potentially limiting generalizability. Future studies could combine online recruitment with offline outreach through LGBTQ±affirming clinics and community organizations, as well as additional platforms beyond WeChat.27 Second, the eligibility window included adults outside the age bands currently prioritized in routine HPV vaccination recommendations and, more recently, in male vaccine approvals in mainland China. As a result, intervention effects on acceptability may not fully generalize to younger, policy-targeted populations. Future work should restrict recruitment to locally approved age ranges or prespecify age-stratified analyses to assess effect heterogeneity. Third, although participants self-identified as gay or bisexual, not all reported having sex with men, which may have introduced heterogeneity in perceived risk and intervention relevance, potentially diluting effects. Fourth, although observed baseline imbalances were adjusted for in primary models, residual confounding cannot be fully excluded. Baseline differences may have influenced responsiveness to the intervention, and future trials should consider stratified randomization to improve balance and strengthen causal inference. In addition, the study assessed acceptability rather than actual vaccine uptake; longer follow-up with behavioral endpoints is therefore needed.16 Finally, structural barriers were not directly addressed. Integrating subsidies, provider partnerships, and stigma-sensitive services will likely be essential to translate psychosocial gains into real-world vaccination.21

In this randomized controlled trial, a brief IMB-guided intervention delivered via a WeChat official account improved short-term HPV vaccine acceptability among unvaccinated adult men in mainland China who self-identified as gay or bisexual, including those reporting sex with men. The intervention’s effects were consistent with IMB theory, operating primarily through strengthening key, modifiable determinants of acceptability – information, social motivation, and behavioral skills – although benefits diminished over time, underscoring the need for reinforcement and implementation support. In the context of China’s expanding access to male HPV vaccination, WeChat-based programs may offer a scalable, privacy-preserving approach to increasing readiness for vaccination among sexual minority men defined by identity or behavior. However, sustained public health impact will likely require booster engagement and linkage to stigma-sensitive, accessible services that address persistent structural barriers.

The authors thank the Center for Disease Control and Prevention in Suzhou, Jiangsu Province, and the MSM-targeted NGO Red Ribbon Social Service Center for their generous support in participant recruitment and community engagement. Their collaboration was instrumental in reaching diverse sexual minority men populations across China. We also thank all participants for their time and for sharing their experiences.

Sin How Lim is Senior Lecturer in the Department of Social and Preventive Medicine, Faculty of Medicine, Universiti Malaya, Kuala Lumpur. He holds a PhD in Epidemiology from the University of Pittsburgh. His research centers on HIV/STI prevention among key populations, tobacco control, and syndemics, using mixed-methods and quantitative approaches.

Li Ping Wong is Professor in the Department of Social and Preventive Medicine, Faculty of Medicine, Universiti Malaya, and Head of the Centre for Population Health (CePH). Her research focuses on social and behavioral medicine, including vaccination, emerging infectious diseases, sexual and reproductive health, and environment–health interfaces. She holds a PhD in Epidemiology from Universiti Malaya.
No potential conflict of interest was reported by the author(s).
All requests for materials and raw data should be directed to the corresponding author.

The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Jiangsu Nursing Vocational College. It was registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR; Registration ID: ChiCTR2400089627) and was conducted without protocol amendments. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. Data were anonymized, and confidentiality was strictly maintained. Given the sensitive nature of the study content, prespecified potential harms included privacy concerns and psychological distress. Participants were informed that they could withdraw at any time without penalty if they felt their privacy was compromised or experienced discomfort.
